patent: Filed January 11, 1950 and issued May 15, 1951 to Richard W. Hamming and Bernard D. Holbrook, assigned to Bell Telephone Laboratories. It is the patent on what are now called Hamming codes. The first part of the text is mathematical: check elements computed as even-parity sums over chosen subgroups of positions, the minimum distance between code groups, and a geometric model in which code groups are vertices of a unit cube. The worked case is the seven-element single-error-correcting code (four information elements m1-m4, three check elements k1-k3), extended by an eighth, overall-parity element to correct one error and detect two. The drawings realise both codes as relay circuits. Hamming published the theory as "Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes", Bell System Technical Journal, vol. 29, no. 2, April 1950, pp. 147-160; Shannon's "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" (Bell System Technical Journal, 1948) had already given the seven-element code as an example credited to Hamming. Single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting codes of this family remain standard in error-correcting (ECC) computer memory. The drawing notation follows Shannon, "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits", Transactions of the AIEE, vol. 57, 1938, which the patent cites.

figs.1: Signal flow runs left to right through the dash-dot blocks. Sending side: switches 1-4 in INP (lower left) operate relays M1-M4; their contacts in M put the four information elements on channels cm1-cm4, and the parity networks K1-K3 ground check channels ck1-ck3 when an odd number of the M relays in their group is operated. Dashed lines are the transmission channels to register RR (MR1-MR4, KR1-KR3). Receiving side: EI operates check relays C1-C3 when their parity group is even; EL is a relay tree on the C contacts that either grounds the check lead (all checks pass) or operates one of E1-E7, the number being the element position (k1, k2, k3, m1, m2, m3, m4); ER passes each register state to output relays OM1-OM4 in OUT, inverted for the channel whose error relay has operated. A box is a relay winding; a cross on a line is a make (normally open) contact, a short bar a break (normally closed) contact; lower-case labels name contacts of the relay with the same upper-case label. The legend states each relay's rule; in the C1-C3 rules M1-M4 stand for the register relays, since EI is wired from contacts mr1-mr4.
figs.2: Two rails, ODD and EVEN, carry ground from left to right. Relay 1 (left) grounds EVEN through its break contact or ODD through its make contact. In each stage between the dash-dot lines A, B, C, D, a relay's break contacts pass the rails straight through and its make contacts cross them, so ground leaves on ODD after an odd number of operated relays and on EVEN otherwise. Boxed numerals 1-N are the relay windings; the dashed rail segments between stage 4 and stage N stand for stages not drawn. Stopped at C with one output kept, it is the network used in K1-K3 of FIG. 1; carried to D, the one used in EI.
figs.3: Replacement receiving circuits for FIG. 1: IE (left) takes the place of EI and LE (right) of EL; ER and OUT stay as in FIG. 1. The top row of IE starts at ground 10 with a crossover chain of the FIG. 2 kind on mr2, mr4, mr3 and mr1, giving the parity of all four information registers on two rails; the following crossover pairs combine it with (mr3, kr1), (mr2, kr2) and (mr1, kr3), so the check lead (upper right) is grounded straight from register contacts when every check group is even. The branches below feed C1-C3, which here operate when their group is odd. LE is the relay tree on c1-c3 to E1-E7 and has no output for the all-checks-pass case.
figs.4: Same layout as FIG. 1 with an eighth element k4, an overall parity check: K4 and channel ck4 drive register relay KR4, and the legend gains KR4 and C4. DEI holds four check relays; C4 covers all eight register relays. DEL is the relay tree on c1-c4 to error relays E1-E8 plus relay RO, which operates when C4 shows even overall parity but one or more of C1-C3 fails, the signature of a double error. Its contacts ro (above the RO box) go to an alarm or stop circuit not shown. ER gains contact e8; INP, M, RR and OUT are as in FIG. 1.

parts.ER: Not named in the text; the correcting contact network between EL and OUT.

glossary.def: One block of binary elements sent together; here seven (FIGS. 1, 3) or eight (FIG. 4) elements.
Information elements (m1-m4) carry the message; check elements (k1-k4) are computed from them so that errors can be found. Element positions are numbered 1-7 in the order k1, k2, k3, m1, m2, m3, m4.
Whether the number of 1s (operated relays) in a group is even or odd. Each check element is chosen to make its subgroup even.
The set of positions one check covers. Every position lies in a different combination of subgroups, so the pattern of failed checks names the position in error.
A code that fixes any one wrong element and flags, without fixing, any two. Here obtained by adding an overall-parity element to the seven-element code.
The least number of positions in which any two valid code groups differ, now called the Hamming distance. Distance 3 allows single-error correction, distance 4 adds double-error detection.
In the patent, the ratio n/m of elements sent to information elements carried.
The patent's term for a binary code whose code groups are arrangements of 0s and 1s; telegraphers called these code combinations.
Relay contacts that close (make) or open (break) when the relay operates. A make and a break sharing one terminal form a transfer contact.
A branching network of transfer contacts on several relays that connects one input to exactly one of 2^n outputs, chosen by which of the n relays are operated.
The lead that, when grounded, lets the register states pass to the output relays. It is grounded either by the all-checks-pass path or by an operated error relay.
House-wiring switches for controlling one lamp from several places; the patent notes that the FIG. 2 parity chain is the same circuit.
